## Learning goals

- I can organize technical evidence so another person can follow my process.
- I can explain calculations, simulations, measurements, code, mistakes, and revisions.
- I can choose a private, classroom, or public sharing method that protects personal information.

## Why this is useful

A final photograph shows what you made. A technical portfolio shows how you defined the problem, tested ideas, found faults, and reached a supported conclusion.

## What you will make

Create one portfolio entry for an existing TEJ project. Use the [student Quarto starter ZIP](../../assets/tej-portfolio/quarto-portfolio-starter.zip) if you can run Quarto. Otherwise, create the same headings in a Markdown file, approved document, or printed report and publish later.

Quarto needs the Quarto command-line tool or an authorized hosted build environment. JupyterLite can edit notebooks, but it is not a replacement for the Quarto CLI and cannot render this website template.

## Before you start

- Choose one completed or current engineering task.
- Gather only teacher-approved evidence.
- Remove student numbers, faces, school account details, classroom codes, private repository links, network details, serial numbers, passwords, and tokens from anything that could be shared.
- Read the starter [README source](https://github.com/mrandrewandrade/tech-edu-resources/tree/master/student-templates/quarto-portfolio-starter) or the README inside the ZIP.

Public publishing is never required. A local render, private submission, or approved classroom file can demonstrate the same learning.

## 1. Tell the engineering story

Use these headings in this order:

1. **The problem:** What need, fault, or question were you addressing? What would success look like?
2. **Initial design or prediction:** Show the first idea and predict an outcome before testing.
3. **Calculations:** Include units, significant figures, equations, assumptions, and an independent check.
4. **Circuit schematic or system diagram:** Use the course drawing conventions and useful alt text.
5. **Simulation or experimental evidence:** Include a labelled table, graph, photograph, or measurement record.
6. **Python analysis:** Link or summarize the notebook when computation adds value. Do not add code only for decoration.
7. **Mistakes and revisions:** Explain one meaningful stumbling block, the evidence that exposed it, and what changed.
8. **Final conclusion:** State whether the evidence meets the original success criteria and identify limitations.
9. **What I learned:** Explain the transferable skill and how you got unstuck.

## 2. Add one project to the starter

1. Extract the ZIP and follow `README.md`.
2. Copy one sample page in `projects/` and rename it with a short lowercase filename such as `motor-current-test.qmd`.
3. Replace the YAML title, description, date, categories, and image description.
4. Replace every sample section with your own approved content.
5. Preview with `quarto preview`. Test navigation, listing search, categories, images, and relative links.
6. Render with `quarto render`. Review the generated site without editing `_site`.
7. Inspect `git status`, then commit the source files and evidence you intended to include.

The starter uses Quarto's native grid listing, category filters, text filter, sorting, responsive layout, and site search. It does not require an external data service or custom JavaScript after publishing.

## The problem

Another student can see the final result but cannot tell why your design changed or whether the evidence supports your conclusion.

**The essential skill:** connect every claim to a calculation, test, observation, source, or limitation.

**The challenge:** add one complete project, one new category, and one revision that materially changed the outcome. Then change the listing order using a documented Quarto option.

**The stumbling block:** a broken image or link may work in the editor but fail in the rendered site because its relative path starts from the wrong source file.

**The investigation:** use the official [Quarto websites](https://quarto.org/docs/websites/), [listings](https://quarto.org/docs/websites/website-listings.html), and [navigation](https://quarto.org/docs/websites/website-navigation) documentation. Search the exact option name and read the YAML example.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 1: concept clue"}
From a file inside `projects/`, count how many folders you must move up before moving into `assets/`. A relative path describes that route.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 2: documentation clue"}
Search the Quarto listing guide for `sort`, `sort-ui`, `filter-ui`, and `categories`.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 3: technical clue"}
For an image stored at `assets/example.svg`, a page in `projects/` uses `../assets/example.svg`. The project list can use `sort: "date desc"` and `sort-ui: [date, title]`.
:::

## Website repair challenges

Complete the challenges your teacher assigns:

- Add your own engineering project and category.
- Change project ordering and explain the configuration option.
- Use the listing's search/filter control to find a category or keyword.
- Repair a broken image and a broken relative link.
- Enable the optional blog, add a post, or remove the blog cleanly.
- Diagnose one intentional YAML or link error using the render message.
- Record the documentation page or search terms that helped.

## Check your work

- Every required section contains project-specific evidence.
- Images have useful alternative text; tables and graphs include labels and units.
- Calculated, simulated, and measured values are clearly distinguished.
- Mistakes are explained as part of the engineering process, not hidden.
- `quarto render` completes and all local links work.
- A private-data review is complete before any sharing.

## Save and submit

Keep the source folder, not only the rendered `_site` folder. If assigned, submit the source repository or ZIP plus the rendered local evidence. Use a teacher-approved identity and sharing location. Publishing to GitHub Pages is optional and follows [Publish Your Quarto Site](../linux-operating-systems/publish-github-pages.qmd).

## Reflection

Which piece of evidence most changed your design or conclusion? What would a reviewer still need to know before reproducing your result?

## Summary

Your portfolio should make the engineering process inspectable without requiring public publication. Continue with [Build a Website with Quarto](../linux-operating-systems/quarto-website.qmd) for authoring details or use Markdown and publish later.
